summary:
Niğde Province stands under the national framework of Turkey. No Niğde-specific signal on trans or LGBTI+ legal exposure was identified in the source inventory; the findings below are national and apply in Niğde.

Homosexuality has been decriminalised since the Ottoman penal code of 1858, and transgender people have been able to change their legal gender since 1988. Turkey has no comprehensive law prohibiting discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation or gender identity, and the European Commission's 2025 report found legal protection insufficient and out of line with the EU acquis.

Same-sex marriage, civil unions, domestic partnerships and joint adoption are not recognised. LGBTQ people are barred from serving openly in the military: the armed forces' health regulation defines homosexuality as a 'psychosexual illness', conscripts who declare it must provide photographic proof, and those receiving an 'unfit report' may face later discrimination in public life.

Pride events have been banned in Istanbul and other cities in most years since 2015, with police using tear gas, water cannons and mass detentions. In June 2025 authorities issued blanket bans against the Istanbul LGBTI and Trans pride marches, police subjected peaceful protesters to unlawful use of force, and over 90 people were arbitrarily detained. Prosecutions of 92 people for participating in pride marches continued at year's end.

In December 2025 an İzmir court ordered the dissolution of the Young LGBTI+ Association after ruling it had shared 'obscene' images incompatible with 'society's moral values'. A court case to close Lambda Istanbul was overruled by the Constitutional Court.

Amnesty International records that three draft law packages targeting LGBTI people were made public during 2025, an unprecedented assault that would criminalise expression of LGBTI identities and consensual same-sex relations and make legal gender recognition nearly impossible; they were ultimately not submitted to parliament. A February 2026 press report of draft legislation criminalising public advocacy of 'behaviour contrary to biological sex' with one to three years in prison was not included in the 12th judicial package, whose passage removed provisions discriminating against LGBTQ people and made symbolic same-sex weddings possible.

ILGA-Europe's 2026 Rainbow Europe ranking placed Turkey 47th out of 49 countries.
tangentialFactors:
The national pattern of pride bans and mass detentions is concentrated in Istanbul and İzmir; no comparable Niğde event or enforcement action appears in the inventory, so a visitor in Niğde should read the national climate rather than a local record of incidents.

Draft legislation has circulated repeatedly through 2025 and into 2026 without enactment, so the legal position a visitor encounters may shift during a stay; whether any further package passes remains unresolved in the sources.
localsOnly:
Niğde residents can change legal gender under the national procedure in place since 1988, but have no statutory discrimination protection on sexual orientation or gender identity and no access to recognised same-sex marriage, civil unions or joint adoption.

Local LGBTI+ residents are exposed to the same national policing practices documented elsewhere in Turkey, including identity checks and detention recorded under 'General Information Gathering' background checks.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Niğde-specific source covers any of the points above; every claim rests on national reporting and is applied to Niğde by extension of the national framework.

Whether the draft legislative packages reported through 2025 and February 2026 have since been enacted is unresolved in the sources.
